# HILLSHADE cross-implementation reference

How `HILLSHADE` reached E4: compared against GDAL 3.13.1, an implementation we
did not write, on the same frozen analytic DEM the slope and aspect references
use. The reference and its provenance are committed here; the steps below
reproduce it.

## Files

| File | State | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `hillshade-gdal.asc` | **committed** | GDAL 3.13.1 Horn hillshade, 8-bit levels, on the DEM's grid. |
| `command.txt` | committed | The exact command that produced `hillshade-gdal.asc`. |
| `environment.json` | committed | GDAL/PROJ version, platform, architecture (no generation timestamp is recorded). |
| `SHA256SUMS` | committed | Checksums, including the shared DEM. |

The DEM itself is **not** copied here. It lives at `../slope/input-dem.asc` and
is generated by `node scripts/make-slope-fixture.mjs`.

## Why the DEM is shared rather than duplicated

One surface, one definition — the same reason the aspect reference shares it. A
second copy could be regenerated or hand-edited out of step with the first, and
then three products would be validated against three different surfaces while
all three READMEs claimed one. `SHA256SUMS` here pins `../slope/input-dem.asc`
by hash, so a DEM that drifts fails the checksum in this directory as well as in
the slope and aspect directories.

The surface is `z = a·x² + b·y² + c·x·y + d·x + e·y`, so the gradient — and
therefore the hillshade — is exact in closed form. Read `../slope/README.md` for
why the coefficients are what they are, and do not simplify them: the cross and
linear terms are what make a north–south flip detectable, which matters for
hillshade for the same reason it matters for aspect. A hillshade is lit from one
compass direction, so a reflected grid is not a permutation of the values — it
lights the opposite flank of every slope and still looks like plausible terrain.

## The two formulas

Both sides implement the standard ESRI illumination model over a Horn 3×3
gradient:

```
h = cos(zenith)·cos(slopeRad) + sin(zenith)·sin(slopeRad)·cos(azimuth − aspect)
```

with `zenith = 90 − altitude`, `slopeRad = atan(zFactor·|∇z|)`, and the sun
azimuth converted from compass degrees into the same math frame the aspect is
expressed in. Our implementation is `shadeFromSlopeAspect` in
`src/terrain/surface/hillshade.ts`.

**The one place they differ is the 8-bit encoding, not the shading.** We write
`round(255·h)`. GDAL writes `round(1 + 254·h)`, reserving level 0 for nodata.
The two encodings of one intensity differ by exactly `(1 − h)` levels, which is
strictly below one level for any lit cell. That difference is deliberately left
**visible** in the reported figures rather than divided out — see "What this does
and does not establish" below, because it is what makes the headline number sit
where it does.

## Producing the reference

```bash
cd tests/fixtures/reference/hillshade
gdaldem hillshade ../slope/input-dem.asc hillshade-gdal.asc \
  -az 315 -alt 45 -z 1 -s 1 -alg Horn -of AAIGrid
```

Every parameter above is GDAL's default, and every one is passed **explicitly
anyway**. A default that agrees today is not a comparison basis: if either side
changed its default the two grids would be lit by different suns, and the
cross-check would report a shading disagreement that is really a parameter
disagreement. The same values are pinned as `SUN` in
`scripts/make-slope-fixture.mjs` and passed explicitly by the test.

The defaults that would silently change the result if altered:

- **`-az 315`** — sun azimuth, degrees CLOCKWISE FROM NORTH. Our
  `azimuthDeg` uses the same convention.
- **`-alt 45`** — sun altitude above the horizon, degrees. Not a zenith angle;
  passing 45 as a zenith would give the same number here by coincidence and a
  wrong one at any other angle.
- **`-z 1`** — vertical exaggeration. This is a *look* parameter, not a unit
  fix; the DEM is metric with 1 m cells, so no unit conversion is wanted.
- **`-s 1`** — ratio of vertical to horizontal units. `-s 111120` is the usual
  value for a geographic DEM and would flatten this projected one to nothing.
- **`-alg Horn`** — the estimator. `-alg ZevenbergenThorne` is a different
  gradient and would not match our kernel or the closed form.
- **No `-multidirectional`, no `-combined`, no `-igor`.** Each is a different
  illumination model. `computeMultiHillshade` in our tree is the multi-light
  variant and is **not** what this reference validates.
- **Edges excluded.** `gdaldem` drops the one-cell border by default and, on a
  Byte band, writes its nodata value 0 there; `-compute_edges` opts in. Either
  is fine — the test drops the border regardless, because our kernel clamps at
  the edge while GDAL leaves it undefined, and comparing there would measure a
  difference in edge policy rather than in shading.

Record in `command.txt` **which binary you ran**, verbatim, not just the flags.

Then:

```bash
gdalinfo --version   # into environment.json, exactly as printed
shasum -a 256 ../slope/input-dem.asc hillshade-gdal.asc command.txt environment.json > SHA256SUMS
```

## Measured agreement

Read off a run of `npx vitest run tests/hillshadeCrossCheck.test.ts`, over the
11,564 interior cells (the one-cell border dropped):

| Leg | Max \|Δ\| | RMSE | Within ±1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| ours vs closed form (unrounded) | 0.0000643 | 0.0000072 | 100% |
| GDAL vs closed form | 0.900 | 0.410 | 100% |
| ours vs GDAL, both 8-bit | 1.00 | 0.536 | 100% |
| ours vs GDAL, ours unrounded | 0.900 | 0.410 | 100% |

Restricted to the 10,932 cells steeper than 2°, ours vs GDAL is unchanged at max
1.00 / RMSE 0.536, so the agreement is not carried by flat ground.

Separately, and with **zero** tolerance: re-encoding our intensity in GDAL's own
scale, `round(1 + 254·h)`, reproduces `hillshade-gdal.asc` **exactly** at every
one of the 11,564 interior cells. That is the strongest statement this fixture
supports, and the test pins it as an identity.

## What this does and does not establish

It compares our hillshade against GDAL's: two implementations of **one**
algorithm. That catches coding errors — a wrong azimuth conversion, a mirrored
aspect, a zenith/altitude swap — and it is why the closed-form comparison is in
the test as well, since two implementations of one method can agree while both
being wrong the same way.

**Read the ours-vs-GDAL tolerance result with care.** The 1.0-level tolerance
was pre-registered before any comparison ran and is not being renegotiated here,
but it is worth stating plainly what it can and cannot detect. Because
`255·h − (1 + 254·h) = h − 1` is always in `(−1, 0]`, the encoding difference
alone consumes up to a full level of a one-level budget, *for any surface*. On
this fixture it spends 0.900 of the 1.0, leaving roughly 0.1 of headroom for an
actual shading disagreement. So the ours-vs-GDAL leg on its own is a weak
instrument: it would not detect a small shading error. The claim rests on the
other two results, which are sharp — agreement with the closed form to 6×10⁻⁵ of
a level, and exact byte-for-byte reproduction of GDAL's raster under GDAL's
encoding.

It does not validate the choice of Horn, it does not validate
`computeMultiHillshade` (a different illumination model, still at its own
evidence level), and it does not touch the point cloud → DTM pipeline, since it
starts from a DEM. It promotes `HILLSHADE` and nothing else.

## Do not

- **Widen the tolerance.** 1.0 on the 0–255 scale is pre-registered in
  `REFERENCE_SLOTS` before any comparison ran. If a future measurement misses
  it, that is a finding about the hillshade implementation, not a reason to
  change the number.
- **Change our encoding to match GDAL's.** `255·h` is what the product ships
  and what the renderer expects. The offset is characterised in the test, not
  engineered away, and no source under `src/terrain/` was touched for this.
- **Divide the encoding difference out of the reported figures.** It would make
  the GDAL leg look perfect and hide the fact that it eats the tolerance budget.
- **Compare against a multidirectional or combined hillshade.** Different model,
  different claim.
- **Have the test invoke GDAL.** It compares against the committed artifact, so
  CI needs no GDAL. Shelling out would break CI everywhere it is not installed.
- **Resample to make the grids line up.** The test requires identical
  dimensions. Resampling to force a comparison invents the agreement.
